analysis.one_liner: Lets states allow heavier trucks on Interstate highways, raising the weight cap to 97,000 pounds.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 1999 and died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law caps most big trucks at 80,000 pounds on Interstate highways. This bill would have let any state allow a six-or-more-axle tractor-trailer weighing up to 97,000 pounds, with heavier axle loads than today's standard, to run on the Interstates. It never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Trucking companies and freight shippers gain the most: a single truck could legally carry roughly 17,000 more pounds per trip, so the same freight moves in fewer loads. States that host heavy industries like mining, agriculture, and manufacturing would get a tool to attract that freight, and consumers might see slightly lower shipping costs pass through.

how_it_helps.text: Amends federal law so any state may allow a tractor and one trailer with six or more axles weighing up to 97,000 pounds, including enforcement tolerances, to operate on the Interstate System.

Sets axle load limits of 34,000 pounds on tandem axles and 51,000 pounds on tridem axles, and requires the trailer to be at least 48 feet long, so the extra weight is spread over more axles than a standard 80,000-pound five-axle truck.
It is a state option, not a federal mandate: each state chooses whether to permit the heavier combination on its Interstates.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the costs would fall on everyone who uses or pays for the highways. Heavier trucks increase crash severity and stopping distance, and pavement and bridge wear is ultimately funded by taxpayers. Railroads, which move much of the same bulk freight, would face more competition from heavier trucks.

drawbacks.text: Raising the gross weight cap to 97,000 pounds puts more mass on the road per trip, which raises crash forces and can lengthen stopping distances; the bill text contains no new safety, braking, or inspection requirements beyond the axle configuration.

Axle loads of 51,000 pounds on a tridem set are heavier than what the current federal bridge formula allows, so bridge and pavement stress would increase in states that opt in, with repair costs borne by highway budgets funded by taxpayers.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill's benefit goes to a specific industry while the costs — road wear and safety risk — are spread across the public; that imbalance is the core objection raised to every truck-size increase.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The industry case is real: more axles under more weight can mean fewer truck trips and potentially less pavement damage per pound of freight than standard five-axle trucks. But the bill's gains are concentrated in trucking and shipping, while the risks — heavier crashes, bridge stress, and repair bills — land on the general public, and the bill includes no accompanying safety or funding measures. As drafted, the benefits to ordinary people were speculative and small, and the costs were diffuse but real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and immediately passed down to its Ground Transportation Subcommittee, where it sat until that Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Merrill Cook introduced the bill on May 4, 1999, together with Rep. Collin Peterson of Minnesota.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
On May 5, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Ground Transportation.
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill never received a hearing or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Highway users and taxpayers are better off because the bill died: no state gained the option to run 97,000-pound trucks on the Interstates, so bridge and pavement stress and heavier crash exposure stayed off the roads. Trucking companies and shippers lost a chance to move more freight per load, and railroads kept their freight mix unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Collin Peterson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alongside Rep. Cook as an original cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never acted on it — no hearing or markup is recorded.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Ground Transportation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 5, 1999 until the Congress ended, with no recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small support was bipartisan — 2 Democrats and 4 Republicans among 6 cosponsors — and there is no recorded opposition vote because it never reached the floor.

industries.note: The bill would let trucking carriers haul about 17,000 more pounds per trip on Interstates, cutting cost per ton. The offsetting costs — road wear, bridge stress, and heavier crashes — fall on the public rather than on carriers.
Shippers could move bulk goods in fewer loads, lowering their freight bills. Their gain in cheaper shipping comes at the public's expense in highway wear.

Heavier trucks are widely understood to shift freight from rail to road, since railroads compete directly with trucking on bulk freight. Railroads' interest in keeping truck weight limits unchanged runs alongside the public's interest in limiting highway wear.
